newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Curtain opens for FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Curtain opens for FOMC meeting.

text.p: U.S. credit market players will wake up on Tuesday with one single thought in mind: What will the Federal Reserve policy makers do with monetary policy at the Federal Open Market Committee September meeting?

Analysts spent most of the day on Monday drawing out scenarios on how the market will react if the Fed decides to leave rates unchanged, raise them by 25 basis points or maybe even increase them by 50 basis points.
But opinions on Wall Street remained mixed.
Matthew Alexy, CS First Boston chief market strategist of fixed-income, said he believes the market is very much neutral going into Tuesday's FOMC meeting.
"This is just sort of a waiting game. There isn't much left to do," Alexy said.

Some analysts said Treasuries have room to rise if the Fed decides to leave monetary policy on hold. The theory, they said, is based on expectations that upcoming economic data are likely to show a slowing economy.

"If you have a relief trade tomorrow, it can then turn into a genuine better sentiment later on due to the fact that you might get weaker data in the next couple of weeks," said Kathleen Stephansen, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
The market will take in a new batch of data over the next few weeks, including key September payrolls on October 4.

Some pundits, however, said they believe the market is in a bear trend and will remain that way regardless the Fed's decision Tuesday. Those experts said Treasuries are likely to drop as a natural consequence if the Fed raises rates.
On the other hand, they said a steady policy decision by the Fed would automatically trigger expectations of a possible rate hike at the November FOMC meeting.

"If they do nothing, the market will have an initial flurry of activity in the front-end. The long-end will probably slowly continue to grind towards higher interest rate levels," said Steve Ricchiuto, chief financial economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd Securities Inc.
"This (a steady policy) would not in any way, shape or form end the bearish sentiment in the marketplace," the BZW economist added.

In the case of a 25 basis points hike in the federal funds rate, which is currently targeted by the Fed at 5.25 percent, Ricchiuto believes the short-end of the curve would begin to price in a possible next tightening in November.
"If they go ... you'll have the front end begin to price in the next move, probably at the November meeting," he said.
A recent Reuters survey showed a slim majority of economists -- 17 out of 30 pundits -- believes the Fed will tighten monetary policy on Tuesday.

Of the remaining 13 respondents, seven projected a monetary policy tightening at the November 13 FOMC meeting, one called for a rate hike early next year and five saw the policy unchanged in the foreseable future.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was quoted up 10/32 at 96-21/32 in late afternoon trade on Monday to yield 7.02 percent.

The Fed added reserves to the banking system on Monday via three-day system repurchase agreements, when the federal funds rate was at 5-3/8. Federal funds are seen opening at 5.31 percent on Tuesday. -- (212) 859-1676
